extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reading MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claims are directed to abstract ideas (or other judicial exceptions) under the Alice/Mayo framework, including how to identify improvements to computer-functionality or other technology and example concepts courts have treated as abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer-functionality or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: The application should disclose sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement, and the claim itself must reflect the improvement in technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the claim covers a particular solution or way to achieve a desired outcome rather than merely claiming the idea of a solution or outcome, and whether the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) is limited to computer implementation. See MPEP § 2106.05(a). Mere automation of manual processes or increasing speed when those improvements arise solely from a general-purpose computer is not sufficient to show an improvement in computer-functionality (see FairWarning, Credit Acceptance). A claim must include more than conventional implementation on generic components or machinery to qualify as an improvement (see Affinity Labs, TLI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve improvement question early in eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the question of whether a claim improves computer-functionality or other technology may be considered in either step of the Alice/Mayo test (Step 2A or 2B), examiners are encouraged to resolve this question as early as possible in the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim directed to a clear improvement in computer-related technology (e.g., Enfish) could be found eligible at Pathway A under the streamlined analysis (MPEP § 2106.06(b)) or at Pathway B as not being directed to an abstract idea. If an improvement is not clear enough for Step 2A, it may still contribute to eligibility in the Step 2B analysis (see Amdocs v. Openet example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must recite an abstract idea to be directed to it
rubrics_metrics.description: The Step 2A analysis requires a claim to recite (i.e., set forth or describe) an abstract idea in order to be directed to that idea, thereby separating claims that merely involve or are based on abstract ideas from those that recite them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind that 'all inventions at some level embody, use, reflect, rest upon, or apply laws of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract ideas' (Alice), but only claims that recite an abstract idea are 'directed to' one for Step 2A purposes. Examine claims for whether they actually set forth a concept similar to judicially-identified abstract ideas before concluding they are directed to an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims based on or involving an abstract idea but not reciting it are not directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Some claims are not directed to an abstract idea because they do not recite anything similar to a judicially-identified abstract idea, although at some level they may be based on or involve an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial decisions (e.g., Enfish; DDR Holdings; Trading Techs.) illustrate that claims improving database structures, modifying conventional Internet hyperlink protocols, or improving GUIs to prevent incorrect order entry can be not directed to an abstract idea when they don't recite a concept similar to those identified as abstract. Non-limiting hypothetical examples (printer, washing machine, earring sensor, BRCA1 sequencing method, BIOS loading method) illustrate claims that do not set forth an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a claim recites an abstract idea, the claim-as-a-whole may still be not directed to it if it recites an improvement or additional elements that shift the focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Some claims that recite an abstract idea are not directed to it because they also recite additional elements (such as an improvement) demonstrating that the claims as a whole clearly do not seek to tie up the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The improvement or additional elements must shift the focus of the claimed invention from the abstract idea that is incidentally recited. Courts have identified such improvements as indicative of eligibility in Step 2A (see McRO, Enfish, Research Corp.). Non-limiting hypothetical examples include surgical shears with a pressure regulator, a robotic arm assembly with sensor-based control for smooth motion, an autofocus camera system with a particular autofocus algorithm and drive mechanism, and an internal combustion engine with exhaust gas recirculation controlled by a processor—each recites specific improvements to how technology operates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on concepts identified in case law, not judicial descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should rely on the concepts identified in the cases, not the judicial descriptors themselves, when determining whether a claimed concept is similar to a concept that the courts have identified as an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associations of concepts with descriptors (e.g., 'fundamental economic practices') are not mutually exclusive and some concepts may map to multiple descriptors (e.g., hedging was described as both organizing human activity and a fundamental economic practice). Use the factual concept in precedent rather than only the label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices are commonly identified as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to the economy and commerce, such as agreements between people in the form of contracts, legal obligations, and business relations, have been described by courts as 'fundamental economic practices' and treated as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include hedging (Bilski), processing an application for financing (Credit Acceptance), rules for conducting wagering games (In re Smith), buySAFE (transaction guaranty), and OIP Techs. (offer-based price optimization). If a claim's concept is similar to these economic practices, treat it with caution under the abstract-idea analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity — managing relationships/transactions/legal obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to managing relationships or transactions between people, or satisfying or avoiding a legal obligation, are a category the courts have identified as often being abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases include buySAFE (transaction guarantees), Dealertrack (managing credit applications/clearing-house processing), and Bancorp (managing life insurance policy values). Such claims can be 'squarely about' contracting or processing information between parties and may be abstract absent a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity — advertising, marketing, and sales activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to advertising, marketing, and sales activities or behaviors have been identified as abstract ideas in case law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Apple v. Ameranth — generating and transmitting menus, or taking restaurant orders, was characterized as an abstract idea and adding conventional computer components did not confer eligibility. Other examples include structuring a sales force (In re Ferguson), using advertising as currency (Ultramercial), and algorithms for business visit optimization (In re Maucorps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity — managing human behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to managing human behavior (e.g., storing user-selected spending limits and notifying when limits reached) have been treated as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (budgeting/spending-limit tracking). Related examples include content filtering (BASCOM) and certain mental processes (In re Meyer). Such claims that are essentially rules or methods for monitoring or influencing human behavior may be abstract unless tied to a technological improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity — tracking or organizing information
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts involving tracking or organizing information (e.g., filtering content retrieved from a network) have been identified as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BASCOM described content filtering as an abstract idea and a method of organizing human behavior. Claims that merely organize or filter information using conventional components may be treated as abstract absent an inventive concept or technology-specific improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-limiting hypothetical examples of claims that do not set forth an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of claims that do not recite an abstract idea include a printer with belt/roller/printhead/ink cartridge; a washing machine with tub/motor/controller; an earring with a sensor for blood glucose measurement and memory; a method for sequencing BRCA1 gene sequences via PCR and sequencing; a BIOS loading method for a local computer requesting BIOS from remote memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate claims reciting concrete physical structures or technical processes that do not set forth judicially-identified abstract ideas and therefore are not 'directed to' abstract ideas for Step 2A purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere automation or speedup using a general-purpose computer is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere automation of manual processes or increasing the speed of a process where these purported improvements come solely from the capabilities of a general-purpose computer are not sufficient to show an improvement in computer-functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite FairWarning, Credit Acceptance. Examiners should look for improvements beyond conventional computer implementation—i.e., changes in how the computer functions or specific technological improvements—rather than mere automation or faster execution on generic hardware.
